name: Philip Grant Holladay
race_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic, identifying within the broad census-style White category.
residence: Laramie, Wyoming, United States. Philip lives with his wife in a comfortable, paid-off house in an established neighborhood. They have a modest yard and a small workroom, but no large property to manage. The former print shop building they retained is a separate property and remains a source of both income and occasional maintenance work.
education: He completed a two-year technical program in printing and later took evening community-college courses in bookkeeping and small-business management. He did not pursue a four-year degree. The practical training helped him move from press work into estimating jobs, managing production schedules, and eventually running a business; he learned much of the financial side by doing it.
long_term_goals: Philip wants to keep enough energy and independence to enjoy travel, stay involved with friends, and remain in the home he and Diane know well. He would like to take a Northeast trip that combines a few days in a walkable city with one baseball game, but they have not chosen a date or itinerary. He also wants to keep their finances understandable and leave room for home repairs and future health needs. He is not trying to turn retirement into a second career or to fill every week with activities.
occupation: Philip is retired from owning a commercial printing and mailing business in Laramie. He started as a press operator, moved into estimating and production coordination, and eventually bought into the company with a colleague. For decades he dealt with customer proofs, deadlines, equipment failures, staffing, and the narrow margins of jobs that looked simple from the outside. He sold the operating business to two long-time employees at 68 and stayed on briefly to help them take over. He retained the building and leases it to the current business. He no longer works a regular schedule, though he occasionally answers a question from the tenants or arranges a repair. He is pleased the shop continued under people who knew its customers, but the roof and heating system still give him more involvement than he sometimes wants.
household_finances: Philip and Diane’s gross household income is generally about $230,000 a year, so it is above $200,000, though investment income varies. It comes from retirement benefits, Diane’s pension, Social Security, distributions from investments built partly from the business sale, and rent from the former shop building. They are financially comfortable, but do not treat that income as an unlimited travel budget: taxes, property upkeep, insurance, health expenses, and preserving savings all affect what they choose to spend. Their home has no mortgage, but occasional building repairs can be substantial.
style: He speaks plainly, with a dry, understated humor. In a group he tends to listen first and will give a concise answer rather than take over the conversation. He becomes more animated when discussing a well-designed stadium, a production problem, or a game he has seen in person. With close friends he teases more freely; with strangers he is courteous but not instantly familiar. He dislikes inflated sales language and asks direct follow-up questions when an explanation seems vague.

personality.description: Philip is self-reliant and practical, with a stronger sentimental streak than he shows at first. He likes tangible results and respects people who know their craft. He can be attached to an itinerary once he has imagined how it will work, but he is not so rigid that he cannot enjoy a change. He is socially comfortable in a small group and less interested in being the center of a large one.

big_five.scale: Fictional descriptive ratings on a 1–5 scale, where 1 is low, 3 is moderate, and 5 is high. These are character choices, not measured psychological scores.

preferences.reading: Philip enjoys reading for leisure most days, often with coffee or before bed. He likes biographies, American history, books about business and the built environment, and mysteries with a strong sense of place. He reads a local newspaper regularly and is happy to read a novel that is simply entertaining. He usually has a paperback near his chair and brings one on trips; he will set a book aside if it starts to feel like an obligation.
preferences.travel: Travel is a shared pleasure for Philip and Diane, who is retired from an administrative job at a local college. In most years they take one trip of roughly a week or longer and a couple of shorter breaks, depending on their plans and what they want to spend. Philip is particularly drawn to baseball parks and the cities around them. For him, a game is not just a chance to follow a team: he likes the shape of the field, the habits of the crowd, the public address and scorekeeping rituals, and the way a park reflects its city. He sometimes keeps a paper scorecard during a game, though he is not trying to document every inning perfectly. He enjoys a game or a stadium visit as one part of a trip, not a reason to spend every day in the stands.
preferences.travel_style: Philip and Diane travel together, but they do not need to share every activity. Diane is more interested in museums, independent shops, gardens, and live theater; Philip is glad to join her and likes exploring neighborhoods on foot between planned stops. They often arrange one afternoon where each can pursue a separate interest, then meet for dinner. For longer domestic journeys they usually fly, and in cities they prefer transit, walking, or a taxi or rideshare over driving and parking. They will use a rental car for a rural extension, but dislike long daily drives that reduce a vacation to moving between hotels. They favor two or three nights in a place over a different hotel every night. A quiet, well-located room matters more to them than a luxury name or elaborate service. Philip is willing to pay for a good view of a game or a convenient hotel location, but is not drawn to premium extras that do not improve the experience. He likes a local restaurant and a comfortable seat after a day out, and is not interested in nightlife as a travel requirement. He chooses seats that allow him to stretch his legs and does not want a whole vacation built around standing for hours.
preferences.recent_trip: In 2025, Philip and Diane spent eight nights between Chicago and Milwaukee during baseball season, attending one game in each city. Philip had sketched out adding a third stop in St. Louis so he could visit another park, but Diane did not want another hotel move and they both wanted time to explore the two cities without watching the clock. They dropped the extra leg. He was disappointed at first: adding another stadium had seemed like the satisfying completion of the route. In the end, he liked having a slower day between games and time to revisit a neighborhood they had enjoyed. He still thinks about the park they skipped, but does not describe the trip as incomplete. The compromise felt worthwhile because their time together was better than the more ambitious plan on paper.
preferences.future_travel: They have talked about a trip to the Northeast, with a game if the timing works and enough days to visit museums and walk around without rushing. It is an idea, not a booked plan. Philip likes traveling in places where public transport and compact neighborhoods make it easy to change the day’s plan. He is open to another international trip, but does not feel compelled to travel overseas just to prove he can; for a long flight, the destination needs to interest both of them.

beliefs.political_identification: Moderately conservative. Philip emphasizes personal responsibility, continuity, and limits on government, while accepting that some public programs and dependable local services are important.
beliefs.convictions: He values keeping commitments, paying people fairly, and treating customers and employees as individuals rather than entries in a ledger. He supports Social Security and Medicare as public programs people have planned around, and appreciates public libraries and maintained roads. He is not a political activist and usually avoids turning a dinner with friends into an argument. He can be skeptical of government spending without assuming every public service is wasteful.

skills: He is good at estimating time and materials, spotting production bottlenecks, negotiating practical compromises, and explaining a complicated process in ordinary language. Years of running a print shop made him comfortable with budgets and operating decisions, but he does not claim to be an investment expert. He is a patient baseball scorekeeper and has a good eye for the way a stadium is laid out. He can handle routine phone and computer tasks but would rather not troubleshoot a new app while standing in a crowded place.
behaviors: He usually starts the day with coffee and the newspaper, then takes a neighborhood walk if the weather and his schedule suit him. He checks in on the rental building’s needs without wanting to be on call for every minor issue. During baseball season he watches games at home and occasionally meets a friend to watch one together. He keeps travel ideas and game notes in a paper notebook, but does not make a minute-by-minute itinerary. On a trip he is more likely to remember a conversation with a fan or a meal after the game than to keep a complete list of attractions.
health: Philip is generally well and manages ordinary errands and city walks independently. He wears glasses for reading and has some stiffness after sitting through a long game or spending a full day on his feet, so he prefers breaks and comfortable seating. He can walk several miles at a relaxed pace, but does not seek strenuous hikes or try to turn travel into an endurance test. He and Diane take routine health appointments and future care costs seriously without treating age as a reason to stop making plans.
relationships: Philip is married to Diane, and they have been together for more than four decades. They have no children and never had children; their household consists of the two of them. Their marriage is affectionate and companionable, with different enthusiasms that they make room for rather than expecting one person to adopt the other’s interests. Diane is often the one who notices when an itinerary has become too packed, while Philip is more likely to want to add one more stop. They have a small circle of long-standing friends, including former customers and business acquaintances, and see some of them for lunch or a game. They also keep in touch with nieces and nephews, but do not have parental responsibilities.
other_facts: Philip still has a sample sheet from an early job at the print shop tucked into a desk drawer. It is not valuable, but he remembers how much care went into getting the ink and registration right. He is proud of having built a business that provided steady work, though he does not introduce himself by his former title now that he is retired.
